title: Which of 1,000 versions broke it?
hook: Version 1 works, version 1,000 doesn't. Do you really have to test them one by one?

knows: that a program changes over many saved versions
doesNotKnow: that any yes/no test that flips once (works, then broken) can be halved
that 1,000 versions need at most 10 tests

misconception: To find which of 1,000 versions broke something you must test them one by one, or about half of them.
objective: The learner can explain that testing the middle of the suspects rules out half of them whatever the answer, so 999 suspects shrink to 1 in at most 10 tests (2^10 = 1,024), provided the break stays once it appears.

claims.text: Testing the middle of the suspects rules out half of them whichever answer comes back: 999 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 63 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1.
claims.source: Demo.tsx testAt()/mid() on the stage's fixed first-broken version v737 (chosen only as a fixed value; 974 of the 999 possible positions also take 10 tests, 25 take 9). Builder re-ran the halving in Node.

claims.text: Halving 999 suspects down to 1 takes at most 10 tests, because 2^9 = 512 is too few and 2^10 = 1,024 is enough.
claims.source: ceil(log2 999) = 10 (Demo.tsx WORST). Builder checked over all 999 positions in Node: max 10 tests.

claims.text: Testing one by one from v2 would have taken 736 tests to reach v737.
claims.source: v2 to v737 inclusive is 737 - 1 = 736 versions (Demo.tsx BAD - 1).

claims.text: The method works only because once a version breaks, every later version stays broken.
claims.source: Assumption of the method: the test result must be monotone over versions (works ... works, broken ... broken). git-bisect documentation describes the same good/bad split.

claims.text: git bisect finds the commit that broke a program this way.
claims.source: git-bisect(1) manual: 'Use binary search to find the commit that introduced a bug' (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-bisect).

claims.text: A test away from the middle can rule out fewer than half the suspects and waste a step.
claims.source: Testing v(lo+1) rules out one suspect if it works (Demo.tsx testNext); the worst case of an off-middle split is the larger side.

recall.question: A bug appeared somewhere in the last 4,000 saved versions and has stayed ever since. With 'works / broken' tests, about how many tests do you need at most?
recall.why: Each middle test halves the suspects, and 2^12 = 4,096 covers 4,000, so 12 tests are enough.
